THE ANSWER TO "IS THERE A RISK OF SOMETHING BREAKING" IS NO, and the reason is worth stating plainly: a missing font cannot break anything. There is no error path - the browser simply falls to the next family in the stack. The only possible symptom was cosmetic, and the check below rules that out too. Zero is a stronger statement than "it did not load" - it means no element can reach it under any circumstance. ## 2026-08-22 20:45 UTC-05:00 · design-decision · fonts/theme-audit
The app ships ten megabytes of typefaces nobody thought were used. Two of the six ARE used - on the Wallach quotation blocks - and the old measurement missed them because a font only downloads when a word using it appears. Four really are dead.
  ↳ Fonts are about half of what a visitor downloads on first visit, so this was the biggest single saving available anywhere in the project. The standing note said six of the thirteen typefaces are never used and cutting them would save 10.2 MB. That note was written from a network recording - a list of what the browser actually downloaded during one session - and a browser only downloads a typeface at the moment a word using it appears on screen. Nobody had opened the pages that use the serif face while recording, so it looked unused. It is used. Playfair, the serif, sets the Wallach quotation blocks: the pull-quote on the Absorption page, the family-designation quote on the essentials pages, and every quoted passage in search results. Deleting it would have quietly turned the app's one deliberate editorial accent into a browser default, on precisely the blocks that carry Wallach's own words. Four faces really are dead. Luneth ruled: cut the two big ones now, keep the two small ones as a hedge in case that voice is ever wanted back. THE NUMBERS, CORRECTED. build_web.py's docstring, the handoff and the 2026-08-21 build-log line all said "6 of 13 shipped faces are NEVER fetched (Merriweather x2 = 9.16 MB, Playfair x2, Crimson x2) ... a real 10.2 MB win". It is 4 of 13, and the approved cut is 8.73 MB off the download / 4.71 MB off the web build (9.21 / 4.88 if Crimson Pro were included; never 10.2). MEASURED TWO WAYS, BOTH STRONGER THAN A NETWORK TRACE. (1) STATIC - every path by which a family can be selected. Merriweather is reachable only through --ds-font-serif and Crimson Pro only through --ds-font-serif-light. Each token is defined in exactly two places, both :root, and type-futurist.css loads later and wins. theme.css declares no --ds-font-* token - VERIFIED by reading it, not taken from the comment that claims it. No JS writes a font token; the picker writes only colour and hue vars. Nothing outside design-system.css names either family. (2) DYNAMIC - drove the app and read the COMPUTED font of every laid-out element, which is the question that matters, rather than what happened to be fetched. Three workspaces, seven knowledge tabs, six entity pages, a condition page, a topic page and search, in cream AND dark. RESULT. Playfair Display x2 is LIVE - both faces "loaded" in document.fonts - on three surfaces in both themes: .kd-ep-fam__quote (Calcium 7, Selenium 9, Zinc 11, Magnesium 7 elements), .kd-foods-pq on Absorption (12), and #drawer-search-mount .vq (79 elements across 201 .vq nodes; type-futurist.css never touches that one, because every selector in it is scoped to #drawer-knowledge-mount). Merriweather x2 and Crimson Pro x2: ZERO computed uses on every surface in both themes, and unloaded after every walk. NEW GATE fonts_declared_and_shipped (board 101 -> 102, consistency 30 -> 31; CLAUDE.md corrected in the same patch, and its own meta-gate caught the stale 101 within one run). Both directions, because a font cut breaks in both: every file in dashboard/assets/fonts/ must be declared by an @font-face, and every @font-face src must resolve to a file that exists. Delete a .ttf and leave the declaration - RED. Delete the declaration and leave the .ttf - RED. The second shape is the silent one: an unreferenced font file renders nothing, errors nowhere and appears on no surface, which is exactly how this rode along unnoticed. WHAT THE GATE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO, written into its own docstring (R7): it does not prove a declared family is ever SELECTED. That cannot be read out of files - the family is reached through a token chain, the token is redefined at :root by a later sheet, and whether a rule matches a laid-out element is a property of the rendered cascade. ## 2026-08-22 20:08 UTC-05:00 · milestone · web/live-host-probe
The website is now checked on the live site after upload, not only before it. Every problem this site has actually had was a hosting setting no local test could see — and it confirmed tonight's upload is serving exactly this build, byte for byte.
  ↳ The download has always been tested here on the machine. The website was assumed to match it. That assumption is the reason the site quietly served yesterday's knowledge base earlier this month while every technical signal said it was fine — because the thing that was wrong was not in the files we built, it was a setting on the server sitting in front of them. From tonight there is a single command that opens the real site and checks it. It also answered the one thing left open from last session: he uploaded at 7:35 this evening, and the live site is byte-for-byte identical to what this repository builds. The fatty-acid ranking fix is live. tools/probes/render_probe_live_host.js (NEW), 33 checks. `node tools/probes/render_probe_live_host.js [url]`, defaulting to https://nutrientcodex.com/. Exit 0 pass / 1 fail / 2 the host did not resolve — a name that will not resolve is this machine or DNS, not a failing contract, and treating that as a failure would cry wolf every time the wifi drops. ★ THE CONTRACT IS READ, NOT RETYPED. Every header assertion is parsed out of the HTACCESS template in tools/build_web.py — the file that GENERATES the .htaccess we upload — so the contract stays in ONE hand-maintained place (§00.B.1). The probe cannot go on asserting a rule after someone changes it, nor stay silent after someone adds one. It also means the FilesMatch ORDER is modelled rather than assumed: the favicon escapes the year-long image cache only because its rule comes later in the file, and that is now proven on the wire instead of by reading the template. WHAT IT COVERS, all of it host-only: .htaccess executing at all (the two Hygiene headers, which no stock server default emits — the NGINX Direct Delivery tell); index.html neither cached hard nor pinned to a long max-age; http to https; Options -Indexes; .htaccess itself unreadable; the .gz trap four ways; every sampled asset carrying the exact Cache-Control its own FilesMatch predicts; brotli on the text payloads; then a real browser on the real domain — zero 4xx/5xx, zero page errors, the corpus counts, the Regimen pager and filter. ★ FRESHNESS IS PROVED TWICE, AND ONE WAY NEEDS NOTHING LOCAL. Every content-hashed asset carries the first 10 hex of its own sha256 in its filename, so re-hashing the DELIVERED bytes tests that claim directly — 12 js/css named in the shell plus the 3 data artifacts, whose URLs exist only inside the bundle and are therefore harvested from what the page actually fetches. A proxy holding the previous deploy's object under this deploy's URL fails right there, with no local build to compare against and no literal that can go stale. The second way, DEPLOY PARITY, runs only when dist-web/ exists and is counted SEPARATELY, because "the host is behind the local build" is a different sentence from "the host is broken". ★ A REAL DEFECT IN MY OWN FIRST DRAFT, CAUGHT BY THE CONTROL: the gzip-magic check read the RAW WIRE BYTES. The actual trap leaves those completely alone — Apache's stock AddEncoding tags an already-gzip file Content-Encoding: gzip, so the stream still starts 1f 8b while the BROWSER hands tesseract.js the gunzipped payload. The check passed cheerfully on precisely the failure it existed to catch. It now reads the DECODED body, which is what tesseract actually receives. ★★ AND A FINDING ABOUT THE EXISTING DIAGNOSTIC, worth more than the probe itself: the "sourced claims" figure on the page is sum(books[].claim_count) — a STORED per-book counter, NOT a count of the claim set (dashboard/assets/js/src/views/knowledge-home.ts:145). It moved during the 2026-08-22 incident only because the stale artifact was a whole earlier build whose counters differed. Two builds can carry identical counters and different claim TEXT, and the count comparison — here and in render_probe_web_build.js — smiles at both. That gap is now closed by the data-artifact self-hash, and the limit is written into the probe beside the check rather than left implied. render_probe_web_build.js was left alone: its artifacts come straight off disk, so they cannot drift there. NOT A GATE, AND IT CANNOT BE (R7): tools/invariants.py must be deterministic and offline, and a gate reaching a third-party host would make the board's colour depend on SiteGround and on whether this machine has wifi. The board stays 101/101. The gate-able half — that the probe and the template agree about what the contract IS — is handled by deriving instead of asserting, which is stronger than a gate would have been. NEGATIVE CONTROLS, 12, EVERY ONE FIRING FOR EXACTLY ITS OWN REASON AND NO OTHER. A control that reds for the wrong reason proves nothing, so each mode names the check labels it must add, and the harness fails on a missing red AND on an unexpected one. A local control host re-serves dist-web/ with one deliberate defect at a time: norules (Direct Delivery ON — 13 reds at once), pin180, gztrap, stalehash, stalecorpus, partial, catchall (a host answering 200 to everything — the instrument's own control), clean (baseline: exactly one red, the https clause a local http host can never satisfy). Plus 3 contract-parse controls proving a reshaped template cannot silence the probe: removed / emptied / headersGone all go RED rather than passing vacuously. ★ THE SHARPEST IS textdrift: ONE CHARACTER of ONE verbatim, swapped for another of the same width. Same counts, same byte length — the rendered-count comparison and the size check are blind by construction, and ONLY the hash of the delivered bytes catches it. Its expectation list is deliberately written to assert what must STAY GREEN; if the count comparison ever appears in it, the control has stopped proving the hash clause is load-bearing. TWO CONTROL ERRORS WORTH KEEPING, both mine and not the probe's. (1) stalecorpus first deleted a claim WITHOUT decrementing books[].claim_count — a shape the real pipeline can never emit, so it was testing an impossible input and the count check correctly stayed green. That is how the knowledge-home finding above was found. (2) partial reported two UNEXPECTED reds; the probe was stronger than predicted — a dropped font surfaces as a 404 response, a console error and a failed request as well as a missing file — so the expectation was corrected, not the probe. AND A HARNESS BUG THAT LIED IN THE SAFEST-LOOKING DIRECTION: the first run reported all 8 modes sweeping clean. The control host lives in the harness process and spawnSync BLOCKS that event loop, so the server never accepted a connection, every mode timed out into NOT_APPLICABLE, and a green sweep of controls had run against nothing at all. Fixed to async spawn, and written into the harness header. MEASURED ON THE LIVE HOST, 33/33 PASS: x-content-type-options + referrer-policy present (Server: nginx, so Direct Delivery is OFF and Apache is in the path); index.html public, max-age=0, must-revalidate; http 301 to https; assets/styles/ 403; .htaccess 403; the OCR model 206 bytes 0-65535/12821300, Content-Encoding ABSENT, application/octet-stream, magic 0x1f8b0808; hashed js/css/json max-age=31536000, immutable and favicon-32x32.png max-age=0, must-revalidate; bundle br 399 KB on the wire; 12 + 3 self-hashes verified; both distributions 2,601 claims / 7 books; 63/63 shipped files resolve AND arrive at their full built size (HEAD with Accept-Encoding: identity, deliberately — with compression negotiated Content-Length describes the compressed response and cannot be compared to disk); 3/3 split artifacts byte-identical to the build. VERIFIED: board 101/101 (24 external / 30 consistency / 45 structural / 2 meta, no new reds — the probe adds no gate); node tools/build.mjs exit 0; render_probe_web_build.js 13/13 still PASS; node --check clean. eslint N/A — tools/probes/ is outside dashboard/eslint.config.js's scope, as every other probe is. HONEST LIMIT, STATED RATHER THAN IMPLIED: it cannot enumerate the SUPERSEDED artifacts piling up in public_html/ (~9 MB, and an overlay deploy never deletes). Options -Indexes is on by design, so there is no listing to read, and a name we no longer ship is a name we can no longer guess. That loose end is untouched and this probe is not what will close it.

## 2026-08-22 19:14 UTC-05:00 · milestone · foods/ranking
The food list was sorted by “most nutritious first” and could not see fats — walnuts, at twice Wallach’s daily essential-fatty-acid amount, sat on page 47 of 64. Fixed in three places, and gated.
  ↳ A serving of walnuts gives you more than twice the essential fatty acids Dr. Wallach asks for in a day. The app knew that — the card printed “220%” in large type — and then filed walnuts on page 47 of 64 in a list whose whole promise is “most nutritious first”. The number on the card and the position of the card were telling a reader two different things. The cause is a small one with a wide reach. Every other essential is scored as its own row: so much calcium against Wallach’s calcium number. The fatty acids are not like that. He states ONE amount for the pair of them — nine grams a day, as flaxseed oil — and never a separate figure for omega-3 or omega-6. So they share a single meter, the way the plant-derived trace minerals do. A score that adds up rows therefore adds up nothing for them. Three surfaces had the same blind spot, and only the first was known when the round started:   1. The default order of all 192 foods.   2. The GOAL order — and this was the worse one. 24 of the 30 goals name omega-3 or omega-6,      so someone who picks “healthy heart” was being shown a list that scored every candidate      as though none of them could do anything about it. It now leads with natto, tempeh and      soybeans, all three of them fatty-acid foods.   3. The card itself, which decided whether to show the fatty-acid figure by re-doing the      arithmetic in its own way and rounding differently. Seven foods rounded UP over the line      and were shown a figure the ranking scored at zero. Two rulings were his, both taken after the alternatives were measured rather than argued. The fatty acids count UNCAPPED, like every other term — capping just that one would have left it the only under-weighted thing in the sum. And they must clear the same 7% bar every nutrient clears to appear at all. A third option, capping everything for symmetry, was measured and thrown out: it pushes beef liver, the strongest food in the catalog by a wide margin, down to third behind lobster. Flattening the big numbers destroys the very signal the cap was meant to protect. What makes this worth writing down is that nothing could have caught it. The board was 100/100. The number was arithmetically correct — correct about the rows it added up. The defect was a term that WAS NOT THERE, which is the one shape a green board, a screenshot and an “is it rendering” check are all blind to at once. It is the same shape as the food sheet’s unstyled Add button from the previous round: absence renders fine. So the fix ships with a gate that recomputes the whole key from the artifact’s own bytes, and the gate asserts the ABSENCE of the cap by existence — it requires a food scoring over 100% and carrying its full excess — because a quietly reintroduced min() would leave every other clause green. The board is 101/101, and the fix was re-broken four separate ways to confirm each one goes red. One more thing the round taught, at my expense. The first version of the probe measured the order in node and told me the app was wrong about three positions. It was not; my prediction was computed before a rounding step the shipped code applies. The same probe then read only the small chips on each card and reported “no fatty acids shown” about precisely the foods that deliver the most of it — because the biggest figure on a card is drawn as the headline, not as a chip. And it read the food list straight after switching goals, without noticing the pager was still on page 7, and confidently named the wrong food as the top pick. Three wrong conclusions in one session, every one of them from reasoning about the app instead of driving it. The corrected probe clicks through all 64 pages.

## 2026-08-22 17:26 UTC-05:00 · milestone · web/probe
The website build is now driven by a probe before upload, comparing its rendered corpus counts against the download build rather than trusting headers.
  ↳ The website build now gets checked by a machine before it is uploaded. Until today nothing ever opened it — the download was tested and the website was assumed to match. That assumption is exactly what let the site quietly serve yesterday's knowledge base earlier this month while every technical signal said it was fine. tools/probes/render_probe_web_build.js (NEW). Serves dist-web/ over a real http server on 127.0.0.1 (an ephemeral port — a fixed one fails with EADDRINUSE against its own previous run in TIME_WAIT and reads as a broken build) and drives it with puppeteer. file:// would not exercise the fetch path at all, which is the entire point: the web build STUBS the three split artifacts out of the bundle and fetches them, so a regression there is invisible on the download and silent on the web. · ★ THE METHOD IS A COMPARISON, NOT AN ASSERTION ABOUT A NUMBER. The corpus counts are read off the RENDERED page in BOTH distributions — the file build, where the corpus is inlined at build time, and the web build, where it is fetched — and required to agree. No literal to go stale, and a build hydrating from the wrong artifact cannot agree with the one that inlines it. That is the diagnostic the 2026-08-22 incident called for and did not have: `curl` and the page's own fetch() of ONE url returned DIFFERENT BYTES, so headers proved nothing. · ALSO ASSERTED: zero 4xx/5xx, zero page errors, and that every fetched assets/data/*.json carries a content hash — a fixed name is a name a cache can serve a stale copy of, which is the whole reason those three carry a digest. Then the surfaces the CSS rewrite could break: the Regimen pager + filter, the mixed catalog with its head agreeing with its grid, a food sheet with Wallach's target column, and the Add button still carrying its fill through the stylesheet rewrite-and-hash pass. · VERIFIED: 13 checks, all PASS against the dist-web built this round — both distributions read 2,601 claims / 7 books (matching seal 491), 3 artifacts fetched and 0 un-hashed. · HONEST LIMIT, stated rather than implied: the local server is NOT a model of SiteGround. The production cache contract lives in .htaccess and can only be verified against the live domain — this proves the BUILD is sound before upload, never that the host serves it right.

## 2026-08-22 17:21 UTC-05:00 · round-close · foods/order+pager+catalog
Foods get one honest order, a real pager with a filter, and a full nutrition label in the Knowledge drawer beside the products.
  ↳ Three changes to how foods work. The list of foods on the Regimen tab is no longer in a puzzling order — it now leads with whichever food fills the most of whatever you have picked as a goal and still have missing, or with the most nutritious food overall when you have picked nothing. Paging through the catalog got a normal pager (1 2 3 4 5 … 64) with a category picker and a name box beside it, so finding a food is a few seconds rather than a few dozen clicks. And every food in the catalog now appears in the Knowledge drawer alongside the Youngevity products, in its own colour, with a full nutrition label behind it. ★ THE ORDER (state/foods.ts, rewritten). Owner ruling 2026-08-22 REVERSES two earlier ones: the eggs pin (2026-08-21) and the greedy walk are both gone, and goals now drive the food order where wantedSlugs() still deliberately ignores them for products. ONE sort key over the whole catalog: with goals chosen it is the share of the OUTSTANDING goal targets a serving fills — Σ min(fraction, 1) over goal ∩ want, over |goal ∩ want| — capped per nutrient because 500% of one target has not filled five. With no goals, or with every goal nutrient already covered, it is `strength` (the food's own Σ of Wallach fractions), which is 'most nutritious first'. Ties fall to strength then to the id, so the order is TOTAL and cannot reshuffle between paints. `greedy`, `education` and `browse` are gone from the signature; `category` and `query` replace them, applied to the POOL so the pager's page count stays derived. The score is a sort key and is never rendered, so its denominator has only to be constant across candidates — a goal naming omega-3 (which no row can credit) dilutes every candidate identically. THIS APPLIES TO COVERAGE TOO: one shared ranker, and two different orders for the same list on two tabs would be worse. · ★ THE PAGER (views/foods-block.ts + dashboard.css). Windowed, and the window STARTS at the current page rather than centring — the owner's literal shape: '1 2 3 4 5 … 64' on page one, '1 … 20 21 22 23 24 … 64' on page twenty. It slides back only at the end, so the last page reads '1 … 60 61 62 63 64' instead of a lonely '1 … 64'. An ellipsis is emitted only between genuine non-neighbours. FOOD_PAGE_CAP=30 is GONE with the squares that needed it (that cap existed because 64 wrapped to two rows); regimen.ts now requests foodCatalogSize() and the page count is derived from the live pool. Coverage keeps its ‹ N/N › arrows, scoped via a new .fs-pager--numbers modifier rather than off .fs-controls — sizing must not depend on whether a filter happens to sit beside it. · ★ THE FILTER. Category select (the catalog's own 11, derived — never a written list) plus a name box, pager left / filter right. views/regimen.ts gained paintFoods(), which repaints ONLY the block: render() replaces the whole workspace, so every keystroke would destroy the input being typed into. buildFoodsBlock marks and restores the caret across its own repaint. ## 2026-08-22 14:24 UTC-05:00 · incident · web/cache-contract
The live site served a superseded corpus behind a fresh bundle — no error, just a wrong claim count — because three artifacts shipped under fixed names. They are content-hashed now, and the contract is gated with three poisons that each red it on demand.
  ↳ The website was serving yesterday's copy of the knowledge base while showing today's app — no error, nothing broken-looking, just a claim count that was wrong and ten claims back on the page that had been removed. The three big data files now carry their own fingerprint in their filename, so a changed file is a different file and no cache anywhere can hand out an old one again. WHAT HAPPENED, MEASURED. After the 2026-08-22 upload the live site read 'Search 2,611 sourced claims' where the local build reads 2,601 — three runs each, deterministic. The live page's own fetch of assets/data/corpus-embed.json returned knowledge_version 490 with 2611 claims; the shipped seal is 491 with 2601. curl of the SAME URL returned the correct file and sha256-matched the build, so the two disagreed on identical bytes on disk. The headers settled it: `x-proxy-cache: HIT`, Last-Modified a day stale, ETag sizing the PREVIOUS deploy's file (0x2d44c5 = 2966725 B against the new 2953976 B). All three split artifacts were stale; index.html was a proxy MISS and every content-hashed asset was fresh. No service worker (checked: 0 registrations, no controller). ★ AND Cache-Control WAS NOT THE FIX. fetch(url,{cache:'reload'}) and {cache:'no-store'} both still returned HIT — those directives govern the BROWSER's cache; an upstream proxy's own object store is under no obligation to honour them. A flush cleared it, but a manual step that can be silently forgotten is not a fix: forgetting it produces a wrong site that looks perfectly fine. · THE FIX: the three artifacts are now CONTENT-HASHED like the JS and CSS have always been. tools/esbuild_web.mjs owns the naming (sha256, first 10 hex, matching build_web.py's digest()), bakes the map into the bundle as --define:__SPLIT_MANIFEST__, and writes a sidecar manifest that build_web.py reads to name the shipped files. ONE hasher, not two: two independent implementations that drift produce a bundle asking for a file nobody shipped. state/data-split.ts fetches pathFor(key) off that manifest instead of a fixed `./assets/data/${key}.json`. build_web.py hard-fails if the bundle names a file it did not write, or if a name does not carry that file's actual hash; esbuild_web.mjs hard-fails if a hash cannot be computed. The chain is now airtight end to end: index.html is never cached hard (must-revalidate, and verified a proxy MISS) → it names the hashed bundle → the bundle names the hashed artifacts → all three change name on any change. `json` therefore joins the immutable one-year group in .htaccess; those three are the only .json the web build ships and every one now carries its own hash. · GATED IN THE SAME PATCH (§00.B.2). split_data_manifest_agrees gained the cache contract: esbuild_web.mjs must define __SPLIT_MANIFEST__, data-split.ts must read it, and the literal `./assets/data/${key}.json` must not return. Three poisons added to tools/tests/test_split_data_manifest.py, which now reds on 8 drift shapes instead of 5 — each one drove the gate red on demand, so it is not vacuous. A regression here is invisible twice: it cannot fail on file:// (nothing is fetched) and it does not ERROR on the web (it just serves yesterday), which is exactly why it needed a gate and not a comment. · FILES: tools/esbuild_web.mjs, tools/build_web.py, dashboard/assets/js/src/state/data-split.ts, tools/invariants.py, tools/tests/test_split_data_manifest.py. · VERIFIED: web build ships corpus-embed.2154893117.json, search/search-index.169c48eae2.json, creators-log-embed.da1bb55373.json (the corpus hash matches the sha256 taken independently off the live host); served over real http, the app made ZERO requests to an un-hashed path, all three returned 200, and it hydrated to 2,601 claims / 7 books with search answering from the hashed index. The sidecar manifest is deleted before packaging — 0 build-scaffolding files ship. File build unaffected (SPLIT_DATA=false, nothing fetched): dashboard reads 2,601 across three runs. Board 100/100, 79 unit tests, dose_scroll 10 checks, food_tile all five clauses, tsc clean, eslint at HEAD parity on data-split.ts (2 = 2). · ALSO CLOSED THIS ROUND: the foods copy review. Every string was read in its exact rendered form — the four gloss variants, the eight source names, 'Omega EFAs', the serving line, the three block notes — and NOTHING was changed. Owner ruled the two disputed chip labels stay as canon derives them ('Vitamin D2 + D3', 'Folic Acid'); the demo's shorter mock-data wording is declined, because hand-writing them would put those names in a second place to drift. Both items the 2026-08-22 handoff had parked are now closed. DEFERRED: the site declares NO favicon — not in dashboard.html and not in index.html — so every visitor's browser probes /favicon.ico, 404s, and the tab shows a generic globe. It is the only 404 on the live site. Raised with the owner, not taken. ⚠ STILL TRUE AND WORTH KNOWING: .htaccess only applies while NGINX Direct Delivery is OFF, and a host setting can revert it — the one-line proof after every deploy is that x-content-type-options and referrer-policy appear on the bare domain (they do today), and that Content-Encoding is ABSENT on eng.traineddata.gz (it is). The proxy cache in front is a SEPARATE layer from Direct Delivery and is the one this patch defeats.

## 2026-08-22 09:52 UTC-05:00 · round-close · foods/second-sources
Seven of the thirteen essentials no food could reach now have real foods behind them, every food number says which published source it came from and how firmly, and the approved tile design is live.
  ↳ Until this round, thirteen of the ninety essentials had no food a person could eat to move them — the app could only ever say "take a supplement". Seven of those now name real foods, and the numbers on screen say where each came from. Iodine points at iodised salt, lobster and ricotta; molybdenum at tofu, snow peas and pumpkin seeds; sulphur at lobster, venison, turkey and chicken breast; silica at dates, green beans and spinach; chloride at salt, cottage cheese and chard; flavonoids at blackberries and strawberries; biotin at peanuts and hazelnuts. Walnuts, which the app scored at zero for essential fatty acids yesterday, are now worth 220% of Dr. Wallach's daily dose. Hover any number on a food card and it names the publication it came from. Where two tables had to be matched up by food NAME rather than by a shared id, the number carries a small "≈" and says plainly that a person paired the two by hand — a close stand-in, not a measurement of that exact item. The half of this round worth remembering is what was REFUSED. Garlic — the food the campaign most wanted, the richest allium in the literature, and one Dr. Wallach names by name — did not make it: a serving of garlic is three cloves, nine grams, and nine grams delivers 6.0% of his sulphur target. It is a flavouring, not a serving. Oysters at 54-67% sulphur were refused because that source measures them raw and ours is cooked. Lamb chop at 42% was refused because their cut is lean and ours is lean and fat, and fat carries almost no sulphur. Boron was acquired, pinned and extracted, then deliberately not used at all: no source we hold measures boron per 100 g, and the one table that exists is per serving without ever saying what a serving weighs. Twenty-five refusals in total, each written down with its reasoning so nobody re-derives the hope. THE TECHNICAL RECORD SECOND-SOURCE SPINE. eden/foods/sources/sources.json gained `nutrient_bindings` — the ONE home for how a pinned payload becomes a number: payload -> extractor -> committed candidate -> join kind -> value kind -> unit -> the words the card uses. Three value shapes: `cell` (one cell, byte-exact), `sum` (Sigma of component ROWS — USDA's per-compound flavonoid rows), `sum_fields` (Sigma of named FIELDS — Doleman splits sulphur in two). All sums in DECIMAL, never float: '147.63' + '19.58' must be '167.21' on every host because that string is what the gate re-derives. sr_legacy_food.csv (the fdc_id->NDB bridge) and USDA water/18:2/18:3/CLA joined the committed extract as `support_nutrients`, deliberately NOT nutrient_map, so an arithmetic input can never be mistaken for a Wallach-targeted essential. TIER IS DERIVED FROM THE JOIN, NEVER TYPED. An id join may be EXACT; a name join is APPROXIMATE forever. The gate REDs the other combination in EITHER the row or the binding, and REDs a name-joined row whose key or reasoning is not in the curation — a matcher's proposal cannot ship as though a person had accepted it. TWO SOURCES FOR ONE ESSENTIAL. Bindings declare `combine`: `sum` where parts measure DIFFERENT things (USDA publishes proanthocyanidins separately from the other flavonoid classes, and omitting them understated every total — 2 qualifying foods became 10), or `first` where they measure the SAME thing and only one may win. Sulphur is `first`: AFCD primary because it measures directly per 100 g, Doleman second because its dry-weight value must be married to a moisture from a different sample. They are complementary rather than competing — AFCD supplies 24 foods, Doleman fills the three it has nothing for (chicken breast, cod, egg). The derive REFUSES to guess: a multi-part binding with no `combine` hard-fails. DOLEMAN, PINNED. Europe PMC serves the CC BY paper as JATS XML, so Table 1 comes out of real table cells rather than PDF coordinates. All 32 rows matched the values that had been hand-typed into convert_sulfur.py exactly — they were right; pinning makes them provable. That script is retired. The dry-to-fresh conversion (umol/g dry x 32.06 x dry-matter x 0.1) happens at derive time because the dry-matter fraction depends on which catalog food the row was paired with; every shipped row carries the umol/g, the water, the fraction and the arithmetic as a sentence. 32.06 lives in the binding AND independently in the gate, so editing one REDs. The rule conflated WHICH measurement to attach (genuinely ambiguous) with WHETHER THE FOOD CONTAINS IT (not ambiguous).   ↳ Luneth reported that hovering a removed-item "Restore" button in the recycle bin made its text almost unreadable on every dark accent. This is the correct fix -- and it also corrects a misfire from earlier today. What went wrong first: last round I "fixed" .rc-btn-restore, which is the deleted-SAVES restore pill -- the WRONG button. His words were "ONLY for removed items", and removed items use a different (ghost) button class, .rc-btn-ghost. Worse, my earlier change hurt the deleted-saves button's own hover contrast, so I reverted it. The real bug: in dark, dark block (G) lifts the ghost button's text to --ds-accent-bright so it reads on its resting translucent wash. But (G)'s :is() selector carries specificity (0,5,0), so it also governs the :hover state. The base :hover (workspace-regimen.css) FILLS the background with the solid accent colour -- and bright-accent text on a solid-accent fill is accent-on-accent, roughly 1:1 contrast (worst on amethyst: purple text on purple). Invisible. The fix (J8, theme.css, dark-only):   :root[data-theme="dark"] .rc-item .rc-btn-ghost:hover {     background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--ds-accent) 32%, transparent);     border-color: var(--ds-accent);   } Instead of filling solid, the hover DEEPENS the translucent tint and solidifies the border, keeping the dark theme's bright-text-on-dark regime. That keeps the bright text readable on all 8 accents. I first tried a single fixed light text (#fffbf2) but it washes out on the pale accents (measured gold 2.06, ember 2.45, teal 2.54 -- below even bold-AA); the deepened-tint approach avoids that entirely. Reverted: J6's .rc-btn-restore:hover -> --ds-accent-hot change from commit 88acd1a3. That button carries dark --ds-paper-light text (#221d15 in dark), so saturating its hover fill actually dropped its text contrast from ~7.5 to ~2.3. Restoring the original --ds-accent-deep hover is better for it. J6 is now the .pf-done fix only. A verification lesson: my first recycle probe INJECTED a top-level .rc-btn-restore button and reported a false PASS. A synthetic proxy at the document root is not the real element in its real container -- and it also let me test the wrong class without noticing. The honest check drove the ACTUAL recycle popup (seeded the bin through the real removal bridge, opened it, hovered the real button) and screenshotted it. ## 2026-08-16 23:56 UTC-05:00 · design-decision · scanner
Scanner hero reframed: 'covers N of 90' (full Wallach targets, ~always 0, a stack funnel) -> the ITEM's 'hits N of 90' (>=3% of Wallach's target). Pumpkin now 'Worth adding · delivers 6 · 2 strongly'. + fixed the Copper->'Pepper' parse bug. 00.A-clean.
  ↳ Luneth scanned pumpkin seeds — one of the most nutritious foods there is — and the scanner said "0 reach the 90 this scan". He pushed back hard, and he was right: the scanner was headlining how many of the 90 essentials a scan got you to FULLY cover (a full Wallach daily target). Wallach's targets are so high that no real food, and no single supplement, hits even one of them alone — only the whole Youngevity stack (Ultimate Daily + EFA Plus + Tangy Tangerine + Ultimate Classic ...) approaches full coverage. So a "covers N of 90" headline is always ~0 and quietly turns the scanner into a funnel to buy the entire program, which is the opposite of its job: helping people judge which foods and supplements are worth introducing. THE FIX, in two parts. 1. The scanner headline is now the ITEM's "hits N of 90" — how many essentials it delivers a MEANINGFUL amount of, defined as >= 3% of the Wallach daily target (his call, grounded on the real pumpkin numbers below). This scales honestly: a whole food hits ~6, a strong multivit far more, the full stack ~90 — so the number actually moves and discriminates. Crucially it is NOT called "covered": 3% is a meaningful start, not a full dose, and the wording says so. The full-target truth still lives on the Coverage tab (where YOU stand); the scanner answers "how good is this ITEM". Two honest jobs. 2. Copper bug: the OCR auto-corrector (ocrFuzzyFix) only skipped words it already knew as food terms, so a recognized nutrient-panel label like "Copper" — which is in the known-nutrients list but not the food-term list — got snapped to the nearest food word, "Pepper" (and "Phosphorus" -> "Phosphoric"), silently dropping them from the scan. Now it also skips anything in the known-nutrients list. 00.A: the 3% threshold is a DISPLAY threshold, always measured against the Wallach target.low (never an RDV/DV), and only the ~38 essentials Wallach has actually dosed are eligible. Where Wallach is silent there is no target to measure against, so the nutrient cannot be a hit (an honest non-hit — e.g. phosphorus, which pumpkin seeds have in quantity but Wallach never dosed). REAL NUMBERS (his pumpkin label through the live engine, % of the Wallach target): Magnesium 20.8, Manganese 18.2, Copper 9.7, Iron 4.3, Zinc 4.3, Potassium 3.6, Selenium 1.6, Phosphorus 0 (no Wallach dose). At >= 3%: hits 6 (Fe, Mg, Zn, Cu, Mn, K) — exactly the set he intuited, including hard-to-get potassium. Strong (>= 10%): 2 (Mg, Mn). His literal "5%" intuition would have given only 2, because Wallach's targets run ~5-15x the RDV — a genuinely useful correction that came out of grounding the number in the real engine. RESULT: pumpkin seeds now read "Aligns · Worth adding · Meaningfully delivers 6 of your 90 essentials · hit in a meaningful amount, a real start not a full daily target · 2 delivered strongly · 0 ingredient flags". FILES: - state/scanner.ts — meaningfulHits() returns { hits, strong }; HIT_THRESHOLD 0.03, HIT_STRONG 0.10; ScanResult gains hits/hitEssentials/hitsStrong (interface only, recomputed per scan). - views/scanner.ts — renderResult(): dropped delta/added/gaps; deck + gauge (single green hit-arc) + caption + facts all reframed to the item-hits story. - workspace-scanner.css — .vd-cov-arc-cov/.vd-cov-arc-add -> .vd-cov-arc-hit. - state/ocr.ts — ocrFuzzyFix skips known nutrient labels (dict.knownLower). VERIFY: tsc + esbuild 0; invariants 91/91 (dead-rule gate green); render_probe_ocr/scan/scanner 0; live re-open render of the pumpkin label screenshotted and signed off. Coverage tab untouched. DEFERRED (Luneth left open): the /90 gauge still reads a bit modest for a food (small green arc) — he may want a more strengths-forward visual later; the caption/deck/"delivered strongly" wording is open to tuning.

## 2026-08-16 21:30 UTC-05:00 · round-close · scanner
WF-cheese ingredient read: scan grabbed the 'DISTRIBUTED BY' text, not the real ingredients, so no villains flagged. Fix: header line-anchored + headerless heuristic (comma-rich run after the last %DV). label-test-2 now flags modified/processed; no regression.
  ↳ The cheese-tub scan (label-test-2) was reading the wrong text as its ingredient list - it pulled the "DISTRIBUTED BY / Whole Foods Market / www..." line instead of the actual ingredients, so none of the bad ingredients (like modified cornstarch) were flagged. Root cause: the OCR garbles the real "INGREDIENTS:" header on this label, and the only clean word "INGREDIENTS" left in the text is the trailing allergen line "CONTAINS MILK INGREDIENTS." - the old regex matched THAT and captured everything after it, which was the distributor block. Fix: the ingredients header must now sit at a line start (so it can no longer match the mid-sentence "MILK INGREDIENTS"), and for labels whose header is garbled the ingredient list is found structurally - it is the comma-rich run that comes AFTER the nutrition panel. Nutrition panels are full of "% DV" and ingredient lists have none, so we slice from the last "% DV" to the end, after cutting off the distributor / contact tail. TECH -- state/ocr.ts parseOcrText: - Header regex line-anchored: /(?:^|\n)[^\S\n]{0,8}(?:OTHER\s+)?INGREDIENTS?.../i (still allows supplement "Other Ingredients:"), plus a reject if the capture starts with distributor/manufactured/packed boilerplate. - New headerless heuristic (only runs if nothing else set ingredients): body = whitespace-collapsed rawText, truncated at the first of DISTRIBUTED BY / MANUFACTURED BY / PACKED BY / www. / http(s) / (c); then start = end of the LAST "% DV" match (fallback: end of the last "Protein Ng"); take body.slice(start), strip leading punctuation, require >=3 commas and 30-2000 chars. VERIFY: tsc 0, eslint 0 errors, build 0 (11597 KB), invariants 91/91 (0 new reds). e2e via window.lcOcrToLabel + lcScan, 0 page-errors: - label-test-2.jpg now extracts the real block ("PROCESS AMERICAN CHEESE (CULTURED MILK, NONFAT MILK, CREAM, SODIUM PHOSPHATE, SALT, COLOR [ANNATTO, PAPRIKA]... MODIFIED CORNSTARCH... NONFAT DRY MILK POWDER, GARLIC, CHILI PEPPERS, VINEGAR, SALT, CITRIC ACID... XANTHAN... CAYENNE PEPPER POWDER"), 513 chars; the anti-flag engine flags "modified / processed" (was 0 flags). - label-test.png ingredients unchanged (654 chars; still flags fried-oils / added-sugar / modified) - no regression. Residual: the head of the cheese block still has OCR garble ("PATRRTED PROCESS" = "Pasteurized Process") - the right ingredients are there and the villains flag; Confirm lets the user clean the garble. ## 2026-08-16 21:08 UTC-05:00 · round-close · scanner
Live-review scanner batch: live nutrient-row feedback + Fat->Oat fix + panel labels; progress bar no longer bounces on rotated labels; comma-segment parsing for horizontal panels. Board 91/91, Luneth sign-off, pushed to origin/master.
  ↳ Three fixes Luneth found while testing the scanner live, all signed off and pushed. 1) LIVE FEEDBACK. He corrected a misread nutrient name and nothing confirmed it worked - no check appeared. Turned out to be three problems: the OCR was mislabeling "Fat" as "Oat" (the auto-corrector snapped the word "fat" onto "oat", both in its dictionary one letter apart); the standard panel labels (Total Fat, Cholesterol, etc.) weren't in the recognized list, so even a correct fix wouldn't show a check; and nothing re-checked a row as you typed. All fixed - "Total Fat" now reads right, corrections resolve to a check, and every keystroke re-checks the row live. 2) PROGRESS BOUNCE. ## 2026-08-14 19:08 UTC-05:00 · round-close · scanner
The scanner now reads labels when you just open dashboard.html — no launcher, flag, or server. A live progress bar exposed the real bug (file:// blocks fetching the OCR model); fixed by bundling the model into a self-contained worker. Plus fail-loud error cards.
  ↳ After the last-wins fix, the scanner STILL hung the first time you scanned — and you were right that a progress bar would expose why. It did: the bar froze at “Load engine”, which pointed straight at the cause. When the app is opened as a plain file (file://), the browser refuses to let the page fetch() its own local language-model file, so the OCR engine never got its model and hung forever. The fix bundles that model directly into the OCR worker, so nothing needs fetching — OCR now works just by opening dashboard.html. Over http (your future online version) it uses the normal lighter path with no bundled bloat. It also fails loudly now: a clear error card with a Try-again button instead of an endless spinner. ROOT CAUSE (reproduced on the real file:// app): the vendored Tesseract worker loads eng.traineddata.gz via (env==='webworker'?fetch:...)(_) — the global fetch. On file:// the browser blocks fetch() of local files (net::ERR_FAILED, 'Failed to fetch'), an uncaught rejection that never settles createWorker, so the Scan step hung on 'Loading the language model'. Everything else loads fine because it uses importScripts (allowed on file://). Confirmed the fix direction two ways: --allow-file-access-from-files made it work (0.5s), and http worked natively — both prove fetch was the blocker. THE FIX — bundle the model, no fetch: - dashboard/assets/vendor/tesseract/worker-offline.js: one self-contained worker = [model base64] + [a self.fetch patch that serves the bundled model to any *.traineddata request] + [the vendored worker.min.js]. Tesseract wraps the worker as new Blob(['importScripts("<abs url>")']); a blob worker CAN importScripts an absolute file:// script (that is why worker.min.js works) but a relative import resolves against the blob base — so everything lives in ONE file with no relative imports. Generated by tools/build.mjs (idempotent; regenerates from worker.min.js + eng.traineddata.gz so it can never drift). git-force-added (~16MB) because the tesseract dir is gitignored and GitHub downloads only include tracked files — the offline-download case needs it present. - state/ocr.ts: workerPath = onFile ? worker-offline.js : worker.min.js (window.location.protocol). The reachability preflight (assertModelReachable, a headers-only fetch) runs on http ONLY — on file:// the model is bundled, no fetch. A 60s withTimeout backstops any stall. Errors surface as typed codes (OCR_MODEL_UNREACHABLE / OCR_TIMEOUT). PROGRESS INDICATOR (concept C, screenshot-approved earlier): - state/ocr emits ProgressUpdate {stage 0|1|2, message, determinate, fraction} via lcscan:progress. - views/scanner.renderScanning() renders the staged pills (Prepare / Load engine / Read label) + bar + note; mount.onProgress updates them in place (no re-render). Setup phases are an indeterminate sweep; the read phase fills with Tesseract's real recognition %. Honest — no fake timings. FAIL-LOUD: - views/scanner: scanError state + renderScanError() card (Couldn't read the label + Try again), shown instead of an infinite spinner; cleared on a new scan. failScan maps the typed codes to plain guidance. VERIFICATION (real app, headless Chromium): - Raw file:// (NO flag / launcher / server): a rendered supplement label read into 3 mapped nutrient rows (Zinc / Vitamin C / Magnesium) in ~2s, 0 page errors — the exact double-click case. - http://localhost: reaches Confirm via worker.min.js:200 + eng.traineddata.gz:200 (the lean online path). - Board 91/91 (offline_no_runtime_network, vendor_assets_pinned, dead-rule + keyframe gates all green). tsc + eslint clean. render_probe_scanner/scan/ocr/adopt + the new render_probe_scanner_concurrency all PASS. HOUSEKEEPING: deleted the two obsolete launcher .bats (launch-/serve-wallach-codex.bat) and the dead-end shim/base64 prototype files; tools/build.mjs now builds worker-offline.js; tools/README updated. SEAL / §00.A: corpus_seal was NOT run. eden/ is untouched this session (clean git status), and eden/corpus/drafts holds 7 UNREVIEWED draft books that corpus_seal would promote into the canon — that needs per-claim review in a dedicated corpus session, never as a byproduct of closing a scanner chunk. Nothing pillar-level changed, so nothing needed sealing; the session is sealed by this commit + this append-only entry. ## 2026-08-14 16:33 UTC-05:00 · round-close · scanner
Fixed the scanner hanging on “Reading the label…” forever when a label image is uploaded and pasted at the same time. The newest image now wins; the older read is dropped. Root cause: two OCR runs double-loaded the engine and wedged the worker so it never returned.
  ↳ When you uploaded a label image and pasted one at the same time, the scanner froze on “Reading the label…” forever. Two scans started at once, both loaded the OCR engine, and re-loading it mid-run jammed the worker so it never returned an answer. Now a newer image simply replaces an older one that is still being read, and any read that fails cleanly resets instead of hanging. ROOT CAUSE (reproduced on the real file:// app with puppeteer): - No re-entrancy guard: an upload + a paste fired together each ran a full OCR pipeline (repro: workersCreated=2). - loadTesseract() early-returned only if window.Tesseract was already defined; on a fresh scanner both concurrent scans saw it undefined and each appended <script src=…/tesseract.min.js> (repro: 2 script tags). Re-running the UMD clobbers the first worker’s module state mid-init, so worker.recognize() never settles → state stays 'scanning' → “Reading the label…” forever, PAGE_ERRORS=0 (a silent never-settle, not a thrown error). - FileReader had a 'load' handler only; an 'error'/'abort' left the same permanent 'scanning'. FIX: - state/ocr.ts: loadTesseract() now caches a module-level in-flight Promise (tesseractLoad); concurrent callers share ONE injection; reset to null on script error so a later scan can retry. - views/scanner.ts: LAST-WINS. A monotonic scanSeq is bumped on every handleImageFile(); the previous reader is aborted; the load handler and the ocrToLabel().then both no-op when seq !== scanSeq, so a superseded scan’s late result can never clobber the current view. failScan(seq, e) is seq-guarded and also handles the reader 'error'/'abort'. imageDataUrl reset at scan start. BEHAVIOUR (Luneth’s call): LAST-WINS — the newest image supersedes any in-flight scan (chosen over first-wins / ignore-the-second). VERIFICATION: - Board 91/91 (0 new reds). tsc --noEmit + eslint (touched files) clean. Build OK, dist/main.js 11446.6 KB. - NEW permanent gate tools/render_probe_scanner_concurrency.js — PASS: one OCR worker from two tight-together inputs, reaches Confirm, winner=paste.png (last input wins), exactly one tesseract.min.js injection, 0 page errors. Real gate: the same measurements read 2 pre-fix. - Existing render_probe_scanner / render_probe_scan / render_probe_ocr / render_probe_adopt all PASS. Screenshots (idle + confirm-after-upload+paste) render clean — no visual regression (the fix is behavioural). - Housekeeping: removed the stale render_probe_journey.js row from tools/README.md (feature deleted 2026-08-13) and added the new probe’s row. FILES: dashboard/assets/js/src/state/ocr.ts, dashboard/assets/js/src/views/scanner.ts, tools/render_probe_scanner_concurrency.js (new), tools/README.md. Wallach's sourcing ladder verified against all 7 books before it ships as doctrine - it holds, but "colloidal" on a label does NOT mean the good kind, and a scanning typo had one chromium number 10x too big.
  ↳ Before telling anyone "buy this form, avoid that one," we had to check that the rule was actually Wallach's. It wasn't verified - it came from a design mockup. So I read every mention of mineral form and absorption across all seven books. The ladder holds. His numbers: ordinary metallic minerals (the carbonate/oxide/gluconate forms in most tablets) absorb at 8-12%, and only 3-5% once you're past 35-40. Chelated forms reach 40-65%. Plant-derived colloidal reaches 98%. The important discovery is the one the mockup missed: "colloidal" on a label does not mean you're getting the good kind. Wallach sorts colloidal supplements into four types, and type 1 - bare "rock flour" from clay, sea beds and glacial milk - is in his own words "in fact a metallic mineral." Products are sold as colloidal today that are exactly that. Only the type made by living plants carries the 98%. He proves it on the Hunza: they absorb barely any of the mineral water they drink, and their longevity comes from IRRIGATING with it so the plants do the conversion. I also found and fixed a scanning error. Immortality said 50-100 micrograms of food chromium yields "0.25 to 5" micrograms usable. Two other books carry that identical sentence with 0.25 to 0.5 - a dropped "0." made the number ten times too big. Luneth ruled four cross-book conflicts. The most instructive: chelated minerals were invented in the 1960s, not the 1940s, even though the two NEWEST books say 1940s. Our favour-the-newest-book rule would have picked the wrong answer. That rule only breaks ties between defensible readings - where outside knowledge shows one side is simply wrong, recency is irrelevant. He also caught me manufacturing a contradiction that didn't exist. I read "no less than 60 minerals" against "no less than seventy seven" as a revision needing a ruling. Both are FLOORS - 77 satisfies "no less than 60." Inventing a conflict wastes his time worse than missing one. ## 2026-08-10 15:28 UTC-05:00 · round-close · element-headers
Germanium headers approved first time - and the one thing that went wrong was a simulation that looked convincing and proved nothing, which took three tries to measure.
  ↳ Germanium has the best origin story of any of the ninety. It existed on paper before anyone had ever seen it: Mendeleyev left an empty square in the periodic table in 1871, described roughly what belonged there, and fifteen years later a German chemist isolated exactly that and named it germanium. The table was ordered well enough that a missing entry was itself information. This pack was approved on the first round, which has not happened for a while. The reason is worth recording: it was built to the standard the rejected phosphorus round forced us to write down - a headline style that is not locked to body-text size, and no panel that draws a picture of the thing its own headline already names. Nothing in the six panels is an illustration of an object. The one real problem was in the panel I liked most. Germanium is a semiconductor: it takes an electron and passes it on, and adding a trace of another element - "doping" - makes it conduct far better. Wallach says the same electron-passing behaviour is what it does inside your cells. So the panel is a field of electrons moving through a lattice, with a slider for doping and a switch that relabels the identical motion from "in a transistor" to "in a cell". It looked right and it was doing nothing. Dragging the doping made more electrons appear, but it also made them travel faster, so they left the far side just as much sooner - and the number on screen at any moment barely changed. A still image of it would have passed any review. The fix was to make doping increase how many electrons there are and leave their speed almost alone, which is also the more honest physics. Then the measuring instrument turned out to be wrong twice, and both times the right fix was in the instrument rather than in the standard it was checking against. First, counting bright pixels under-reports the effect badly, because once electrons are close together their glows overlap and stop adding up - it reported a twelvefold change as twofold. So the check now reads the number the simulation itself is tracking, as well as what reaches the screen. Second, electrons appear at random, so a single instantaneous reading is just luck; two settings that genuinely differed measured almost the same. It now averages six readings at each setting. Neither fix involved lowering the bar. ## 2026-08-10 14:22 UTC-05:00 · round-close · element-headers
Phosphorus headers approved on the second try - and the first round's two failures turned out to be mechanical, not matters of taste, so both are now written down.
  ↳ Phosphorus is the odd one out among the ninety: it is the only nutrient whose recommended amount is zero. Wallach says you already get far too much of it, and that the surplus quietly drags calcium out of your bones. So this card's whole job is to explain a number that looks, at first glance, like missing data. The first six designs were rejected outright. Two of them were called childish clip-art and the other four read as walls of text. What makes this worth logging is that neither problem was really about taste - each had a specific, findable cause, and both had bitten before: The walls of text happened because the headline style used by every previous header is locked to a small size by a rule elsewhere in the stylesheet. Written that way, a headline comes out at roughly the size of body text, so a panel reads like a document no matter how good the writing is. Larger sizes were available the whole time and had gone unused across four rounds. The fix was to stop borrowing that style and write a new one. The clip-art happened because two panels drew a picture of the thing their own headline already named - broccoli under a headline about broccoli. That teaches the reader nothing they had not just read, and at this size a hand-drawn object always looks cheap. The reference material Luneth collected contains no pictures of objects at all; it is entirely typography and abstract light. The replacement panel takes the story of how phosphorus got its name - it was boiled out of urine in 1669 and glowed in the dark - and instead of drawing a glowing lump, it makes the word PHOSPHORUS itself give off light as you drag the room dark. Nothing is drawn. Two smaller lessons about trusting instruments. A label collision of eighteen pixels sat in the first round while the automated check reported no collisions and my own estimate said it cleared; only measuring the actual positions found it. And in the second round my own overflow check raised a false alarm on a glow layer that is deliberately wider than its frame but invisibly trimmed by it - so the check now tests what is actually painted rather than what the box measures. Separately, the research file for phosphorus was wrong by roughly a factor of three - it described thirteen source passages where the sealed corpus holds thirty-four, and three of its warnings about what could not be quoted were false. It had missed the best material in the element, including the food table and the naming story. Corrected in place. Sodium is where Wallach stands furthest from mainstream medicine, and the trap is that you can quote him into either position and both quotes are real. His 2015 book says salt does not cause high blood pressure and that restricting it will shorten your life. His own 1995 sodium toxicity table lists hypertension, edema, congestive heart failure and renal failure. A panel built on either sentence alone would misrepresent him. So one panel prints both lists side by side, unedited, and states inside the figure that the same author wrote them nineteen years apart. He does reconcile them, but only by moving the cause: he argues the salt sensitivity seen in high blood pressure comes from restricted calcium and potassium rather than from the salt. That reconciliation sits in the closing paragraph rather than being smuggled up into the headline, and every panel touching blood pressure or salt restriction carries a note saying plainly that this contradicts consensus and is not advice. Someone on a prescribed low-sodium diet for heart failure could land on this page, and the page should not read as permission. ## 2026-08-06 16:29 UTC-05:00 · milestone · gate/no_duplicate_questions
Shipped no_duplicate_questions (board 89 -> 90): two claims on one entity page can no longer ask the reader the same thing. Threshold-free, 29 known cases allowlisted in-gate with reasons that expire.
  ↳ The duplicate cards Luneth kept finding now have a machine that catches them, which is the only thing that actually ends this. Every previous pass fixed instances; the class survived because the detector was structurally blind to it. WHAT THE GATE ASKS. Not "are these claims similar?" -- that needs judgement and a threshold, and both drift. It asks the one question that is decidable: do two claims on the same entity page ask the reader the same thing? Bucket by subject and normalised question; a bucket with more than one claim is a violation. Normalisation lowercases, strips punctuation, drops a small stopword list and sorts the remaining tokens, so a reordered restatement still collides while genuinely different content words do not. No score, no tuning, nothing to drift. WHY A SECOND GATE INSTEAD OF FIXING THE FIRST. no_duplicate_claims puts the book inside its bucket key and additionally demands that one quote literally contain the other. Fixed safe_write, the primitive every write in this project depends on: it silently rewrote line endings and its own verify could not see it — and neither could the gate built to catch exactly that.
  ↳ Every file change in this project goes through one tool. That tool had a flaw it was structurally unable to notice. When it saved a file it quietly changed the invisible marks that end each line, and when it read the file back it changed them again in the opposite direction. Its own "did this save correctly?" check compared those two equally-altered copies, so it answered yes no matter what was really on the disk. Three things followed from that. It converted files to a different line-ending style without being asked, which is why 554 files in this project now sit in a style the repository itself does not store. It could never convert a file the other way, because the fix was undone by the very save that was meant to apply it -- so an earlier session was told a save succeeded when it had changed nothing whatsoever. And the sizes it reported were counts of characters while the message said bytes, which is very likely what made that session read a real, successful write as a no-op. The part worth remembering is the second discovery. There was already an alarm whose entire job was to prove this tool writes exactly what it is handed. It had been green for months. It read the file back with a low-level call that, on Windows, silently applies the very same alteration as the save -- so it was auditing the tool using the tool's own blind spot. It was filed under the one category of check this project says can catch a value that is wrong but consistent with our own files, and it could not have caught this. A check that shares the defect it is testing is not a check. So the alarm was repaired first, and deliberately run against the still-broken tool to watch it fail, before the tool was touched at all. Otherwise "it passes now" would have proved nothing. TECHNICAL RECORD tools/safe_write.py -- Path.read_text / Path.write_text default to newline=None, i.e. Python's translated-newline space: LF -> CRLF on write and CRLF -> LF on read. The round trip was symmetric, so the `landed != new_content` verify compared two translated strings. All disk I/O now routes through two new functions, _read_exact and _write_exact (raw bytes plus an explicit UTF-8 codec), which are the only places the module touches file content -- translation cannot be reintroduced by a future edit without deleting them outright. The step-5 verify and the post-swap readback compare bytes and print a line-ending census next to the sizes, because equal LENGTHS never implied equal content. safe_replace, safe_append, check_file, _read_payload are byte-exact; --payload-stdin reads sys.stdin.buffer. Returned sizes are true byte counts. Because matching is now byte-exact, an LF payload will not match a CRLF file. That failure is deliberate and loud: a new _newline_hint names line endings as the cause and says which style to restage with, and stays silent on a genuine content miss. `check <path>` now prints a file's ending census so a caller can stage correctly in the first place. tools/invariants.py -- _read_via_os now passes | O_BINARY. On Windows os.open defaults to TEXT mode, so os.read translated CRLF to LF; the gate's "independent" readback applied the same transformation as the write. check_safe_write_canary now compares raw bytes, carries LF, CRLF, a lone CR and non-ASCII in its probe payload, and asserts the reported size is a true byte count. NEW GATE board_claims_match_reality (consistency) -- CLAUDE.md's "what a green board actually means" section retyped the gate total and the external-anchor count that invariants.py computes: a canonical value in two hand-maintained places, which section 00.B rule 1 forbids. It had already rotted -- the doctor sweep added two gates and the contract kept saying 85 / ~21 while the board ran 87 / 23. The gate reddens on a mismatch AND on a reworded claim, so it can never go green by losing its subject. NEW tools/test_safe_write_byte_exact.py -- 16 cases. Three are load-bearing: they re-break the primitive on purpose (a translating write, caught by the byte verify; a symmetric translation that corrupts the intent too, caught by intent_check; a character-count return, caught by the size assertion) and assert the canary goes red each time. A test that only showed today's code working would have passed just as happily on the broken version. Docs reconciled in the same patch: CLAUDE.md 85->88 gates and ~21->23 external; the write-discipline skill's "Known defect in the primitive" section replaced by the byte-exact contract, with rule 4 and Windows quirk 3 rewritten (payloads match the TARGET's endings, not always LF); chronicle/next-chunk.md no longer carries this as the open bug. VERIFIED. Pre-fix negative controls reproduced all three recorded symptoms: a pure-LF payload landed CRLF and reported 17 for a 20-byte file; a CRLF->LF repair returned OK having changed zero bytes; a lone CR produced "intended=3B landed=3B" on a failing check. The re-codified canary went RED against the broken primitive ("intended=136B landed=136B") and GREEN after ("byte-exact round-trip OK (140B; LF, CRLF and lone CR all preserved)"). board_claims_match_reality went RED against the stale contract ("doc says 85, board runs 88; doc says 21, board has 23") and GREEN after. test_safe_write_byte_exact 16/16, exit 0. node tools/build.mjs exit 0. invariants 88/88, zero reds -- 23 external, 23 consistency, 40 structural, 2 meta. LEFT FOR LUNETH. 554 working-tree files are CRLF only because this bug made them so; git stores LF for every one of them (core.autocrlf=input), and .gitattributes records that this same mechanism already broke the design-system.css seal once. Normalising the tree to LF would make payload staging uniform, but it touches nearly every file in the repo, so it was not done unilaterally.

Neither passes newline=, so both run in Python's TRANSLATED newline space: the write turns every LF into CRLF on Windows, and the read turns CRLF back into LF. The round-trip is symmetric, so the :139 landed != new_content verify PASSES while the disk bytes differ from what the caller intended. That explains both reported symptoms exactly. (a) "reported OK while changing ZERO bytes": a CRLF->LF repair is structurally impossible through this path, because the replacement happens in LF space and the write re-CRLFs it, yielding a byte-identical file and a cheerful OK. (b) "failed its own intent check with intended=1917147B landed=1917147B": a LONE CR (not part of a CRLF) survives the write untranslated but becomes LF on universal-newlines read - same character count, different content, hence equal numbers on a failing comparison. Separately, every size in those messages is len() of a STRING, i.e. characters, while the message says "B on disk": this append reported 1,923,135 B where the file is actually 1,950,744 bytes. That mislabel is very likely what made a previous session read a successful write as a no-op. NOT FIXED ON PURPOSE. safe_write is the primitive every other write in this sweep depends on (section 17). Patching it mid-sweep risks corrupting the sweep itself. It gets its own chunk at the end, with newline="" on both ends, a real byte count, and a negative test that fails if the round-trip stops being byte-exact. WHAT THE CLASS IS. A typeset subscript digit that OCR flattened into a comma or a lookalike letter. Live on user-facing surfaces until now: "Vitamin B,," for B12 (14 times), "Vitamin B," for B3/B6, "(B,)" for (B6), "LDso"/"LDSO" for LD50, "Vitamin 81" for Vitamin B1. A destroyed vitamin number is not cosmetic -- it is the identity of the nutrient the reader is being told about. THE AMBIGUITY THAT MADE THIS A READING JOB RATHER THAN A RULE. A comma in "B,," can be TWO destroyed digits, or ONE digit plus a real comma. Both shapes are live in the same book: "Vitamin B,, discovered in 1879 and isolated in 1932, is a key cofactor" resolves to "Vitamin B2," -- subscript 2 plus a genuine appositive comma -- while "the primary forms of B,, are methylcobalamin" resolves to "B12", two digits and no comma. Nothing but the page distinguishes them, and both readings were confirmed by page reads at 20-40x. ★ 11 HITS WERE NOT DEFECTS. Fixed 6 more vision-verified quote defects (kv=443) and found the five detector classes sit on a dropped-space class from tight justification — real, confirmed by eye, UNKNOWN size: my attempt to measure it returned 387 almost-all-legitimate candidates.
  ↳ Two things this pass. Six more broken quotes are fixed — including the last defect in the pregnancy anecdote Luneth first reported, which now reads correctly end to end. And the five detector classes turned out to sit on top of a bigger problem that I could not measure, which matters more than the six fixes. THE FINDING. Our text says "magnesium at2,000 mg". The page says "magnesium at 2,000 mg" — with a space. Same story for "zinc at 5-15 mg b.i.d." (we had zincat5-15mgb.i.d.) and "fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d." (we had 5gmt.i.d.). Let's Play Doctor is tightly JUSTIFIED: the typesetter squeezed the thin spaces to make lines fit, and the OCR dropped them entirely. On those same pages I can read "andelectrolytes", "ratherthan", "allthree" — all letter-to-letter, and therefore invisible to every one of the five detectors, which only ever see the letter-to-digit and camelCase EDGES of that class. I TRIED TO MEASURE HOW BIG IT IS AND MY MEASUREMENT WAS INVALID. I wrote a vocabulary detector — a token that is not a word but splits cleanly into two words — and it returned 387 candidates across 326 claims. Almost every one was a legitimate word the speller simply does not know: cofactor, peroxidation, subluxations, anticarcinogenic, Framingham, Reichstein, epigenetics. It was the same trap as the lowercase_line_start detector I threw away earlier today, which flagged 69% of the corpus because a verbatim is a mid-sentence slice of wrapped prose. So the honest position is: the dropped-space class is REAL, confirmed by eye on three separate pages, and of UNKNOWN size. Publishing a number would be worse than publishing none, because the number would be wrong and would be quoted back later as if it were measured. The consequence is the part to carry forward. Promoting the five classes to gates does not make the corpus clean of dropped spaces. It makes it clean of the EDGES of that class. That is still worth doing — an edge caught is a defect caught — but it has to be stated plainly, or a green board will imply a cleanliness nobody established. This is the same shape as the limit already written into frontface_verbatims_clean: a mechanical gate holds a floor, it does not certify a page.
